blocks.text: The merge invariant needs monotonic starts: after sorting, every unseen interval starts at or after the current interval's start. If the next start is inside the active interval, extend the active end to the maximum end; otherwise the active interval can be emitted because no future interval can reach backward to overlap it. Sorting equal starts by descending end is not required for correctness when max(end) is used, but it makes containment visible immediately and provides deterministic output. End order and length order do not establish the emission boundary needed by this scan.

messages.text: End order does not make starts monotonic. A later interval can begin before already emitted output, so a single active-tail merge can miss containment.
Length gives no monotonic spatial boundary. Long and short intervals can appear anywhere, so adjacent processing does not justify emission.

feedback.reason: Start order guarantees that no unseen interval begins before the current one, which makes it safe to extend or emit one active interval.

constraints: The downstream algorithm needs a local scan with a justified emission or conflict boundary.

blocks.text: Consider a long interval far to the right and two short overlapping intervals far to the left. Length order may process the right interval first, then move backward, invalidating any decision that previously emitted output. Conversely, a long interval can contain many shorter intervals, but length alone does not say which one starts first. The correct key follows the state that the scan must make monotonic: starts for merging, event coordinates for a sweep, or finish times for a specific greedy selection proof. Comparing key computation cost misses the real issue because all of these comparison sorts have the same asymptotic bound.

messages.text: Both use comparison sorting and normally cost O(n log n). The failure is semantic, not asymptotic.
A tie-breaker can make any key deterministic. Determinism does not make length order support the required invariant.

constraints: The intended output is the union represented as non-overlapping intervals.

blocks.text: With end sorting, the implementation first emits [2, 3) and [4, 5). When [1, 10) arrives, it overlaps both, but a tail-only merge can revise only the last output, leaving [2, 3) incorrectly separate. Start sorting yields [1, 10), [2, 3), [4, 5); each subsequent interval is contained in the active interval, so no emitted output must be revisited. The counterexample diagnoses the universal-end-sort heuristic without claiming that finish-time order is never useful. It is useful when the objective and proof are based on earliest completion, not when the scan represents a union.

messages.text: The late [1, 10) reaches backward across output already emitted. Last-output comparison cannot repair an order that permits backward starts.
That happens to help this example but provides no general monotonic-start guarantee for other positions and lengths.

feedback.reason: The failure occurs because end order allows a later item to start before previously emitted intervals. Start order removes that backward reach.

blocks.text: Sorting by coordinate alone creates groups but does not define the order inside a group. Under [start, end), the ending interval is no longer active at t, while the starting one becomes active at t. Processing the decrement first preserves that meaning. If the algorithm aggregates all deltas at a coordinate and never observes intermediate state, it can use a grouped proof instead, but that is an explicit alternative contract—not permission to leave ties unspecified. Closed intervals reverse the order because both intervals occupy the shared coordinate.

This creates a transient overlap at a coordinate excluded from the ending interval and can inflate the peak resource count.

blocks.text: Start sorting guarantees that every earlier booking begins no later than the current one. If any earlier booking can still be active, the one with the greatest end captures that possibility, so compare `current.start < latestEnd`. Tracking only the immediately previous end is unsafe: after `[1,10), [2,3)`, booking `[4,5)` does not overlap `[2,3)` but still overlaps `[1,10)`. Equality `current.start == latestEnd` is legal under `[start, end)` because the earlier booking excludes its end. Under closed intervals, the same state would pair with `<=`. Sorting determines which bookings are earlier; endpoint semantics determine equality; `latestEnd` preserves containment.

messages.text: Length is unrelated to whether the current start lies before the greatest exclusive end among earlier bookings.
The equality case represents legal adjacency under `[start, end)`; `<=` would create a false conflict.

feedback.reason: After start sorting, the current booking conflicts with an earlier one exactly when its start is strictly before the greatest earlier end.

blocks.text: The insertion algorithm partitions the existing sequence into intervals strictly before the new range, intervals overlapping the growing new range, and intervals strictly after it. Start order makes those regions contiguous. Because the list is also pairwise disjoint, once an interval begins after the merged new end, every later interval does too. Re-sorting by end or length weakens that guarantee and is not a harmless alternative. If the input invariant is untrusted, validate or normalize it first; do not silently assume a different ordering and then apply the same scan.

blocks.text: The per-interval comparison and its possible emission are one loop step, not two globally ordered phases. Sorting must precede any emission because it supplies the proof that a future interval cannot reach backward into committed output.

feedback.reason: Start sorting must occur before state initialization and emission because it supplies the monotonic-start proof used by every later step.

constraints: Objective A merges the union of intervals.

blocks.text: For union merging, nondecreasing starts ensure future intervals cannot reach behind emitted output. For maximum-cardinality unweighted interval scheduling, earliest finish leaves the most remaining room, and an exchange argument justifies the greedy choice. These are different problems even though both use intervals. The transfer rule is to state what must become monotonic or locally optimal before choosing a key. 'Sort by end' and 'sort by start' are neither universally correct nor universally wrong; each needs an objective-specific proof.

messages.text: Union merging is not selecting one interval; it must preserve every covered point. End order does not support the active-tail union invariant.
Chronological starts support merging, but the maximum-cardinality selection proof relies on choosing the earliest finishing compatible meeting.
